title: Biweekly Office Cleaning Cost: Every-Two-Weeks Pricing, Visit Math, and Contract Pitfalls
seoTitle: Biweekly Office Cleaning Cost (Every 2 Weeks): 2.17-Visit Pricing
metaDescription: Biweekly office cleaning cost: 2.17 visits a month at a 1.16x rate premium, about $1,133–$1,888 for 5,000 sq ft. Compare quotes and run the calculator.
excerpt: Every-two-weeks service bills 26 visits a year, which averages 2.17 visits per month rather than a flat two, and carries about a 1.16x per-visit premium. Here is how to price it by square footage, what 14 days of soil means for your space, and how to word the contract so biweekly is not misread as twice weekly.
quickAnswer: Biweekly (every two weeks) office cleaning runs about $0.104–$0.174 per sq ft per visit for 2,500–9,999 sq ft offices and $0.139–$0.232 for suites under 2,500 sq ft, using a 1.16x multiplier. Because there are 26 visits a year, the monthly average is 2.17 visits, so a 5,000 sq ft office pays roughly $1,133–$1,888 per month. It suits offices of under 10 people with light food use and in-house trash handling.

blocks.text: First, define biweekly in the contract

Biweekly is one of the most misread words in janitorial procurement. To a facility manager it usually means every other week. To some vendors and many office staff it means twice a week. The cost difference is roughly 3.4x on the monthly invoice, so the proposal should state the visit count in numbers: 26 visits per year, one visit every 14 days, on a named weekday. If a bid says biweekly without a visit count, ask before comparing it to other quotes.

The second definition issue is monthly billing. Fifty-two weeks divided by two gives 26 visits, and 26 divided by 12 months is 2.17 visits per month. Vendors who bill a flat monthly fee should be using 2.17, not 2.0. A vendor who quotes per visit will invoice three visits in about four months of the year and two in the rest, which is fair but makes budgeting lumpy.
Rates below apply the national size-bracket benchmarks with a 1.16x frequency multiplier, which sits between monthly at 1.28x and weekly at 1.08x.

blocks.caption: Biweekly office cleaning cost by size: 1.16x multiplier, 2.17 visits per month
headers: Effective rate per sq ft per visit

blocks.text: Moving from monthly to biweekly lowers the per-visit rate about 9.4%, from a 1.28x to a 1.16x multiplier. On a 5,000 sq ft office that drops each visit from $576–$960 to $522–$870. The monthly total roughly doubles, from $576–$960 to $1,133–$1,888, because you are buying 2.17 visits. Going the other way, stepping up to weekly cuts the per-visit price another 6.9% to $486–$810 but raises the monthly total to $2,104–$3,507.

The practical read: biweekly is where the per-visit premium starts to flatten out. The jump from monthly to biweekly buys a meaningful cut in soil load per visit for a modest per-visit saving. The jump from biweekly to weekly buys a smaller per-visit saving and nearly doubles spend again, so it should be justified by occupancy, not by rate.

Fourteen days is long enough for three problem areas to cross from routine to restorative: restroom fixtures, breakroom sinks and microwaves, and entry carpet. Everything else, including private office dusting and conference tables, holds up reasonably well for two weeks in a low-occupancy space.

items: Six people on site five days a week generate about 60 people-days of soil per biweekly cycle, a load most crews clear within the quoted time.
Twelve people on the same schedule generate about 120 people-days. Restrooms and breakroom need in-house attention midweek or the vendor's time will overrun.
Entry carpet without walk-off matting will gray along traffic lanes by day eight to ten; a 3 ft by 10 ft mat at the door captures much of the grit.
Restroom urinals and toilet bowls build mineral scale in hard-water regions within about ten days, so descaler dwell time should be built into the biweekly scope.

blocks.title: Sanitary waste between visits
blocks.text: Feminine hygiene receptacles cannot wait 14 days. Under OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030), any employee assigned to empty them needs training, gloves, and a documented procedure. Many biweekly accounts either contract a separate sanitary bin service or install hands-free step-on cans and assign liner changes to a trained staff member.
What staff need on hand between visits
A biweekly contract succeeds when the office treats the vendor as a reset crew and handles the daily basics itself. That means having the right containers and a place to consolidate waste.

items: Rubbermaid Slim Jim Step-On 18-gallon bin in each restroom: the foot pedal and internal hinge keep hands off the lid, and the quiet-close lid suits medical or shared-wall suites.

Rubbermaid Brute 5-Caster Dolly under the central barrel: rated to 250 lb, twist-lock fit for 20 to 55 gallon Brute containers, so the person on trash duty rolls one barrel to the dumpster instead of carrying bags.

Rubbermaid Traditional Janitorial Cart 6173 for the vendor's visit or an in-house porter: 25-gallon vinyl bag, 300 lb capacity, and a front platform that holds a mop bucket so the restroom-to-breakroom circuit happens in one trip.
A posted midweek checklist: empty desk bins into the central barrel, wipe the microwave and sink, refill restroom paper and soap, and spot-vacuum the entry mat.

items.name: Normalize the visit count
items.text: Convert every bid to a per-visit price and to an annual price at 26 visits. Flat monthly bids divided by 2.17 should land near the per-visit numbers in the table above.

items.name: Check the multiplier
items.text: Divide the per-visit price by your square footage and by the bracket base rate. A result well above 1.16 suggests the vendor is padding for soil risk; ask what they expect to find.

items.name: Itemize add-ons
items.text: Restroom detail runs $15–$30 per restroom per visit, breakroom sanitation $12–$25, and interior glass $15–$35. At 2.17 visits, two restrooms add about $65–$130 a month.

items.name: Confirm insurance and supervision
items.text: Require a certificate of insurance naming you as additional insured, and ask how often a supervisor inspects. Biweekly accounts get skipped more often because a missed visit leaves a 28-day gap.

items.name: Write a make-up clause
items.text: Specify that a missed or holiday visit is rescheduled within two business days rather than credited, so the soil cycle never stretches to four weeks.

faqs.q: Does biweekly office cleaning mean twice a week or every two weeks?
faqs.a: In commercial janitorial pricing it almost always means every two weeks, or 26 visits a year. Because the word is ambiguous, write the visit count and weekday into the contract. Twice-weekly service is 8.66 visits a month and costs roughly 3.4 times as much for the same space.

faqs.q: Why is biweekly billed at 2.17 visits per month instead of 2?
faqs.a: There are 52 weeks in a year, so every-other-week service produces 26 visits. Dividing 26 by 12 months gives 2.17. A flat monthly fee calculated on 2.0 visits would underpay the vendor by about two visits a year, and a fee on 2.5 would overcharge you.

faqs.q: How much does biweekly cleaning cost for a 3,000 sq ft office?
faqs.a: At the 2,500–9,999 sq ft bracket rate of $0.09–$0.15 and a 1.16x multiplier, each visit runs about $313–$522. Over 2.17 visits that averages roughly $680–$1,133 per month before restroom or breakroom add-ons.

faqs.q: Are carpet extraction and floor refinishing included in biweekly service?
faqs.a: No. Routine biweekly scopes cover vacuuming, damp mopping, dusting, trash, restrooms, and breakroom surfaces. Extraction, strip-and-wax, and burnishing are periodic work, commonly amortized at $0.03–$0.06 per sq ft per month or quoted per event.

faqs.q: What chemical documentation should a biweekly vendor leave on site?
faqs.a: Under OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, any chemical stored in your janitorial closet should have a Safety Data Sheet available and labeled secondary containers. Ask for SDS sheets for disinfectants and descalers, and request Green Seal GS-37 certified general-purpose cleaners if your building has sustainability goals.
